macro_reasoning: Wild salmon, not farmed, which the menu specifies and which matters: wild sockeye/coho runs leaner. Portion assumed 7 oz cooked (200 g) = 340 kcal, 45 g protein, 15 g fat, 3.2 g satfat, ~190 mg intrinsic sodium; add 1 tsp grill oil (+40 kcal, 4.5 g fat) and salting to ~540 mg sodium. Arugula salad dressed with lemon and olive oil, 90 kcal, 8 g fat, 1.5 g fiber, 90 mg sodium. Haydari 3 oz (85 g) — Turkish süzme is strained full-fat yogurt, so 110 kcal, 7 g protein, 7 g fat, 4.2 g satfat, 3 g lactose, 210 mg sodium; this is where most of the saturated fat comes from, not the fish. No bread, no rice, no pilav anywhere in the build, which is why fiber lands at only 2.2 g — arugula and dill are the whole plant contribution. Restaurant publishes no nutrition.
why_it_scores: The second Turkish entry earns its place by not repeating the first: no bulgur, no pide, no rice — a char-grilled wild salmon şiş that arrives on arugula and nothing else. It is the only plate in this sweep with no starch on it at all. The haydari follows Turkish mezze logic and does the same job the compendium's cacık does at Bosphorus.
on_flavor: Charcoal on oily fish is the best argument in Turkish grilling: skin blisters, the fat renders into the char. Arugula is peppery and bitter, lemon is aggressive, the strained yogurt is thick and garlicky. Almost nothing is declined except the bread basket. The gap is fibre and vegetables — this plate is fish, leaves and yogurt.

Cooking fat: none added; charcoal rotisserie renders rather than adds, and the only fat is the bird's own skin. why_it_scores: The sides are the whole story: two are included, and black beans and house salad sit in the same price tier as fries and white rice. on_flavor: Real charcoal does real work: the skin browns properly, the ají panca and cumin in the overnight brine push through, and a low soy savour sits underneath. What you surrender by refusing the ají verde is most of the richness — it is mayonnaise with green chile, and it is worth roughly a point of flavour against a point of health.

Steam Vegetables side assumed 150 g with a little butter: 90 cal, 3 g protein, 4 g fiber, 1.5 g satfat. Totals 545 cal / 57 g protein / 9 g satfat. Water crackers refused, so no refined carbohydrate is counted. Restaurant publishes no nutrition data.
why_it_scores: Ordered steamed rather than brown-stewed, this beats the compendium's three existing Caribbean entries by a wide margin. A whole snapper in a thyme-and-pimento broth is fifty-seven grams of protein for well under six hundred calories. The butter in the broth is the only meaningful fat; skipping the rice and the water crackers does the rest.
on_flavor: Everything comes from the broth: thyme, pimento, scallion and a whole scotch bonnet bobbing in it, with okra thickening as it sits. There is no char and almost no acid, which is exactly why it scores where it does. Losing the crackers that normally soak up that broth costs a little texture.

why_it_scores: A wood oven and a long-fermented dough do something no assembled bowl can, and the protein is genuinely respectable — buffalo mozzarella and a 250-gram dough carry it past thirty-five grams. Leopard-spotted char off a sixty-second bake, san marzano acidity, the lactic tang of buffalo mozzarella against long-fermented dough, basil oil released by residual heat, and the wet-centre-against-blistered-cornicione texture the whole format exists for. Nothing was stripped out to make it score.
